short: What an item was worth when it was damaged: replacement cost minus depreciation.
body: Actual cash value (ACV) settlements pay what the thing was worth on the day of the loss, not what a new one costs.
example: A 10-year-old roof costs $18,000 to replace; with 60% depreciation, an ACV settlement is $7,200 before the deductible.

short: A person or company added to your policy so they are also protected by it.
body: Landlords and general contractors often require to be named as additional insureds on a business's liability policy.
example: A landlord asks to be listed on the café's BOP before the lease is signed.

short: An insurance company that has authorized an agency to sell its policies.
body: An independent agency is appointed with many carriers; a captive agent represents one.
example: Pennowick is appointed with ten carriers (story).

short: An agent who sells policies for one insurance company only.
body: A captive agent can compare that company's options but cannot shop your coverage elsewhere.

short: A one-page summary that proves a business has coverage, for a landlord or customer.
body: A certificate does not change the policy. It shows limits, dates and any additional insureds.
example: A general contractor asks the electrician for a certificate before work starts.

short: The first pages of a policy, listing who is insured, what, for how much and for how long.
body: When someone asks for your coverage limits, the declarations page is what they need.

short: The part of a covered loss you pay before insurance pays the rest.
body: Higher deductibles lower premiums. Wind and hail often have a separate percentage deductible.
example: A $4,000 claim with a $1,000 deductible pays $3,000.

short: The loss in value from age and wear.
body: Depreciation is what separates an actual cash value settlement from replacement cost.

short: A change to a policy that adds, removes or alters coverage.
body: Water backup, scheduled jewelry and rideshare driving are all common endorsements.
example: Adding water backup coverage of $25,000 to a homeowners policy.

short: An agency that is appointed with several carriers and can shop coverage among them.
body: The agency works for the client when choosing a carrier, and is paid a commission by the carrier that writes the policy.

short: The most a policy will pay for a covered loss.
body: Policies have several limits: per occurrence, aggregate, and sublimits for specific items.

short: Extra living costs while your home cannot be lived in after a covered loss.
body: Covers the difference between your normal costs and the hotel, meals and laundry you would not otherwise pay.

short: A year-end check of payroll or sales that adjusts a business policy's final premium.
body: Workers' comp and general liability are commonly audited.
example: Estimated payroll $410,000; actual $462,000; additional premium due on the difference.

short: What it costs to repair or replace damaged property with new material of like kind, without subtracting depreciation.
body: Most homeowners policies settle the dwelling at replacement cost, once repairs are done.

short: A smaller limit inside a policy for a specific kind of property or loss.
body: Jewelry theft, cash and firearms often have sublimits on homeowners policies.
example: A $1,500 sublimit for jewelry theft on a $300,000 contents limit.

short: A separate deductible for wind and hail, often a percentage of the dwelling limit.
body: A 2% wind and hail deductible on a $400,000 dwelling limit is $8,000.
